transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-09 15:30 UTC, duration ~68 minutes. Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sara Gomez (Redwood SE), James Alvarez (Nexa Head of Platform), Rina Kobayashi (Nexa SRE), Liam O'Connor (Nexa Security), Maya Patel (Nexa Product)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everybody uh thanks for joining. quick agenda - deep dive on multi-region routing, failover playbooks, we wanna cover policy routing, regional capacity, KV cache behavior, batching and quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem notes.

[00:22] James Alvarez: Great thanks, um our main driver is resilience for inference during region outages and predictable tail latency. we run a mix of user-facing chat and async batch jobs. current stack is GCP primary, with AWS as possible DR region, and we use proto endpoints right now - sorta ad-hoc.

[00:40] Priya Nair: Cool. At a high level Redwood's approach is policy-based routing: you can define rules by latency SLO, cost threshold, or region preference. there are automated fallbacks to compatible model variants if the exact model version isn't available in the target region.

[01:05] Rina Kobayashi: quick question - when you say "compatible model variant" what does that mean for weights/quantization? we need identical output for audits.

[01:18] Priya Nair: Yeah great Q. compatible variant means same model family and version but possibly different precision/quantization profile, e.g., FP16 in region A vs 8-bit quant in region B. logs flag when variant used, and you can set policy to only allow exact-match versions for compliance-sensitive routes. there's also a model-checksum metadata field in the route decision so you can opt-in to strict enforcement.

[01:45] Liam O'Connor: logs flagging is okay but we need cryptographic verification - do you support artifact checksums + signed manifests?

[01:54] Sara Gomez: yes we integrate with customer KMS for manifest signing in Private mode and Redwood Dedicated can validate signatures on model fetch. in Hosted we offer attestations and audit logs, and for Private you can bring-your-own signing key.

[02:20] Maya Patel: what happens to the KV cache on failover? we rely on a prefix cache to keep latency low for chat sessions.

[02:33] Priya Nair: Important one. by default KV (K V) cache is local to the serving plane in a region - we don't replicate hot KV entries synchronously across regions because of write amplification and consistency complexity. instead we use a warmed-cold approach: when a failover occurs, requests are routed to the recovery region and Redwood can warm the KV cache via proactive replays or background prefix prewarming using recent conversation state shipped via secure transfer. there will be a short tail latency spike while cache warms.

[03:05] James Alvarez: That tail latency spike is our top concern for user-facing sessions. any numbers?

[03:12] Priya Nair: In our benchmarks, cold-start tail for chat context is typically 150-400ms extra p95, depending on sequence length. with proactive warming (we can stream last N KV entries to the failover region), we can reduce that to ~20-60ms. caveat: prewarming has network and KMS overhead in Private/VPC setups.

[03:45] Rina Kobayashi: Is the prefix transfer encrypted in transit and at rest? we have strict PII handling.

[03:52] Sara Gomez: yes encrypted in transit using TLS 1.3 and at rest using customer-managed KMS. for Private we don't persist any PII in the control plane unless you opt in; logs can be redacted.

[04:10] James Alvarez: Walk me through a failover scenario step by step.

[04:18] Alex Chen: Sure, typical flow: 1) health detection (Region A crosses failure threshold) -> 2) policy evaluation (route rules choose Region B) -> 3) preflight checks (model availability, capacity, variant matching) -> 4) traffic drain and cutover with header to client indicating fallback -> 5) optional KV prewarm and feature flags to degrade gracefully (e.g., lower beam size or switch to quantized model) -> 6) monitoring and automated rollback / re-route when Region A recovers.

[04:50] James Alvarez: health detection - how aggressive is the detection, we don't want flapping.

[04:58] Priya Nair: We use a multi-signal health detector: control-plane metrics, edge-level latency spikes, and synthetic pings. thresholds are configurable with hysteresis windows; default is 3 consecutive probes across 30s and capacity threshold checks. you can tune it for your tolerance.

[05:20] Maya Patel: on cutover, do clients see a changed latency header or guidance for retry backoff?

[05:27] Alex Chen: Yes we add X-Redwood-Region and X-Redwood-Model-Variant headers, and we emit an advisory event to your observability endpoint. clients see a short-lived 429/backoff pattern only if capacity is saturated; otherwise it's transparent. we also support sticky routing per session if you prefer.

[05:50] Rina Kobayashi: Capacity - how do you ensure Region B can take the load? we're not buying dedicated in both regions.

[05:59] Priya Nair: two patterns: 1) reserved dual-region capacity (Dedicated) where you reserve buffer capacity in multiple regions; or 2) burst-to-hosted policy where region B can burst to on-demand hosted pools but with backpressure thresholds. cost vs latency tradeoff: reserved capacity keeps tail latency low, hosted burst is cheaper but you may see slightly higher latency and cold caches.

[06:30] James Alvarez: Any recs for cost-effective posture?

[06:35] Priya Nair: For Nexa I'd recommend dedicated primary and a small reserved standby in the DR region sized for your 95th percentile failover throughput, plus hosted burst for extreme spikes. that gives predictable headroom without committing to full peak in two regions.

[06:55] James Alvarez: ok that sounds doable. another question - batching and quantization: do you recommend aggressive batching in DR?

[07:05] Priya Nair: Batching reduces per-token cost and improves throughput but increases latency. In DR we often use shedder policies: route latency-sensitive traffic to low-latency paths (smaller batch sizes) and route less-sensitive batch jobs to high-batch lanes. Quantization helps reduce memory and increases concurrency; the tradeoff is a small delta in output quality. for audit/clinical workloads, we generally recommend evaluation with your prompt sets.

[07:40] Maya Patel: can we set per-route quantization policies? e.g., exact FP16 for diagnosis route, 8-bit for general feedback route.

[07:48] Sara Gomez: Yes per-route model profiles are supported. the route definition can pin model.version and model.profile (quant=8bit|fp16) and you can also set fallbacks (deny, allow-degraded, allow-with-flag).

[08:05] Liam O'Connor: On VPC/on-prem: If we bring Redwood Private, is routing still managed by Redwood control plane or do we run a local controller?

[08:15] Alex Chen: For Private you get a control plane piece that can be customer-hosted (air-gapped option) and a local router that enforces routing policies. the default is that you can keep all routing decisions local to your VPC but still receive updates from Redwood's console if you choose. we support hybrid where sensitive routes are evaluated locally and others by the managed plane.

[08:40] James Alvarez: What about billing and accounting when traffic crosses regions or uses hosted fallback? we need clear cost attribution.

[08:48] Priya Nair: We provide token-level cost breakdowns with region and model-variant tags; billing exports can be scoped by project and region. for dedicated contracts we can map usage to the reserved capacity pools. hosted burst is billed separately and labeled.

[09:10] Maya Patel: You mentioned DR playbooks earlier. can you share the template?

[09:16] Alex Chen: Absolutely - we'll share a DR playbook template. key sections: detection criteria, failover steps, prewarm steps, degraded-mode config (lower beam, lower context length), communications plan, and rollback criteria. we'll drop the template and an example spreadsheet with benchmark numbers.

[09:38] Rina Kobayashi: Let's talk instrumentation: what traces/logs do we get during failover?

[09:45] Sara Gomez: You get per-request traces with region hops, model variant, KV-warm status, queueing time, and kernel-level metrics (if Dedicated) like GPU utilization and OOM events. there are also aggregated dashboards for p50/p95/p99 latency by route and region.

[10:05] James Alvarez: About KV consistency - are there any options for cross-region synchronous replication if we really want zero divergence?

[10:12] Priya Nair: Technically possible but not recommended at scale because of latency and write costs. for extremely strict cases, we offer an optional synchronous KV replication mode in Private deployments where you run a cross-region consensus with strong consistency, but expect higher write latencies and cost. most customers prefer eventual consistency with prewarming.

[10:38] Maya Patel: For the benchmark you propose, what test harness do you need from our side?

[10:44] Priya Nair: Provide a representative traffic CSV (timestamps, route, seq length, user-id hash), sample prompts for your top 100 conversations, and target SLOs. we'll run a failover simulation: 1) baseline in-region, 2) cut link and route to DR region, 3) measure p50/p95/p99, cold vs prewarm, and token costs. we'll share a spreadsheet and query-level traces.

[11:12] James Alvarez: Ok we'll produce the traffic CSV.

[11:20] Alex Chen: Anything else on compliance?

[11:24] Liam O'Connor: Yeah auditors ask about replayability of failover decisions for post-incident review. can you provide immutable event logs?

[11:32] Sara Gomez: Yes audit logs are append-only and we provide a signed export of routing events, health triggers, and model-version checks. for Private deployments you can keep logs in your own S3/GCS + we crypto-sign them.

[11:50] Rina Kobayashi: Any gotchas with model-cache eviction when you shift traffic? we worry about mass eviction storms.

[11:58] Priya Nair: We mitigate with staged warmers and soft limits; cutover doesn't immediately evict everything. we also support session-stickiness to reduce thrash and a progressive ramp (e.g., 10% -> 50% -> 100%) during automated failover windows to allow cache warmup.

[12:20] James Alvarez: How mature is the automation? can we run a synthetic "chaos" test monthly?

[12:28] Priya Nair: Yes, Redwood has a runbook automation engine that can run scheduled failover drills, validate SLOs, and auto-generate a postmortem with traces and suggested remediation. we'll partner with your SREs to run an initial drill.

[12:45] Maya Patel: Good. On model variants and evaluation - we'll need to run our clinical prompts against the quantized variants. do you help with eval harness?

[12:53] Sara Gomez: Absolutely, we have an eval harness and scoring templates, and we can run A/B with statistical tests to show regression deltas. we also support gating the rollout using canary percentages tied to quality thresholds.

[13:15] James Alvarez: Anything else? let's recap next steps.

[13:20] Alex Chen: Recap: 1) Alex to share routing policy/DR playbook template and example spreadsheet, 2) Nexa to provide traffic CSV and SLOs, 3) Priya to run failover benchmarks and share results, 4) schedule follow-up runbook walkthrough. We'll also provide security docs and signed audit log options.

[13:40] Rina Kobayashi: Thanks all, that was helpful.

[13:44] Liam O'Connor: quick note - please include a short note on the signed manifests and KMS flow for Private.

[13:50] Alex Chen: will do. thanks everyone.

[13:55] Meeting ends.
